question: The utility replaces the transformer that feeds your plant. Under MTS Appendix C, which studies need updating?
choices: Only the incident-energy analysis
Only the one-line and the load-flow study
All five studies
Only the short-circuit study
explanation: A change in the utility or source is one of the rows in Appendix C that triggers every study. Available fault current changes, so everything downstream of it changes too. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: Nothing in a facility has changed, but the last engineering update was five years ago. MTS Appendix C calls for updating:
choices: Every study, including coordination and load flow
Only the coordination study
One-line, short-circuit, and incident energy
None of them until something changes
explanation: Appendix C ties the five-year mark to the one-line, short-circuit, and incident-energy columns. It does not mark coordination or load flow for that row. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: Which change does MTS Appendix C list as an example of a change in system impedance, configuration, or loading?
choices: Adding power-factor correction capacitors
Repainting the switchgear
Replacing a revenue meter with the same model
Relabeling panel schedules
explanation: Note 1 of Appendix C lists examples such as transformer kVA or impedance, conductor size or length, motor additions, high-efficiency motors, and power-factor capacitors. Each one changes fault current or flow. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C note 1.

question: One project document lists the calculations, design decisions, and product selections the engineer used to meet the owner's goals and the governing codes. ECS calls this document the:
choices: Basis of Design (BOD)
Owner's Project Requirements (OPR)
Commissioning plan
Energization plan
explanation: The BOD explains how the design meets the OPR and the applicable codes and standards, in narrative and itemized form. The OPR states what the owner needs. The commissioning plan organizes the commissioning work itself. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.3 and Appendix A.

question: The owner's document says the data center must ride through a utility loss with no interruption to the critical load, lists budget limits, and defines how success will be measured. In ECS terms this is the:
choices: Basis of Design (BOD)
Short-circuit and coordination study
Final commissioning report
Owner's Project Requirements (OPR)
explanation: The OPR states the functional requirements and how the owner expects to use and operate the facility: goals, measurable performance criteria, cost considerations, benchmarks, and success criteria. The BOD is the designer's answer to it. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.2.

question: Under ECS-2024, who should develop the commissioning plan, and when?
choices: The electrical contractor, after all ATS acceptance tests pass
The commissioning authority, starting in design
The utility, at the time of service energization
The owner's maintenance staff, after turnover
explanation: ECS has the commissioning authority start the plan in the design phase. The commissioning team then updates and expands it through construction, acceptance, and occupancy. Everyone works from the latest version. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.4.2 and 6.4.3.

question: ECS divides the general commissioning tasks into pre-energization, energization, and post-energization. Which task belongs in post-energization?
choices: Verifying that temporary protective grounds have been removed
A thermographic survey under load per Section 9
Developing a written energization plan
Verifying CT circuits have a single point ground
explanation: The infrared survey needs load, so it comes after energization, along with post-energization fluid and gas analysis and load checks. Removing grounds is an energization step. The energization plan and CT checks are pre-energization tasks. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.1.A, 7.1.B, 7.1.C.

question: Under ECS-2024, which item is the owner's representative responsible for giving the commissioning organization?
choices: Timely notice of deficiencies found during commissioning
The final commissioning report
A calibration program for test instruments
Current IED setting files and relay logic diagrams
explanation: Section 4.1 puts the studies, setting sheets, IED setting files, logic diagrams, as-built plans, OPR, and BOD on the owner's side. Deficiency notices, the final report, and instrument calibration are the commissioning organization's job. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 4.1 and 4.2; 5.3.

question: The electrical contractor who installed a new substation offers to commission it with its own crew to save money. ECS-2024 says the commissioning organization should be:
choices: An independent third party
Any firm that holds the installation contract
The equipment manufacturer's field service group
The installing contractor, if a PE signs the report
explanation: ECS requires an unbiased, independent third-party commissioning organization that regularly does electrical commissioning. The installer can't objectively evaluate its own work. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 3.1.

question: Every component in a new lineup passed its ATS acceptance tests. Under ECS-2024, why isn't commissioning finished yet?
choices: ATS results expire after 30 days and must be repeated
ECS requires each ATS test to be repeated at a higher voltage
The system must still be proven against the OPR and BOD
Commissioning only begins after the first year of operation
explanation: ECS builds on ATS: individual components are validated by factory and field tests, then interconnections and the system are tested in part and in whole. Post-energization includes confirming the whole system behaves as the OPR, the BOD, and the approved sequence of operations call for. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 1.1.1, 6.1.3, 7.1.C.8.

question: Which item must the ECS-2024 commissioning report include?
choices: Only the issues that were resolved before turnover
The test technicians' certification exam scores
An issues log with open and closed items
A copy of every manufacturer's catalog
explanation: The report includes the final commissioning plan, test results, systems that don't meet the OPR, a resolution plan for incomplete tasks, as-left IED settings, progress reports, and an issues log with both open and closed items. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 5.4.

question: A new 69-13.8 kV substation has transformer differential protection. Beyond relay testing, ECS-2024 lists which medium-voltage tasks around the differential scheme?
choices: Through-fault primary injection, then operate and restraint checks
Only a visual check that the 87 relay is powered
A dc withstand of the CT secondaries, then a relay self-test at energization
Disabling the 87 during energization until load reaches 40%
explanation: For medium voltage, ECS adds verifying differential schemes per the OPR and primary-injection through-fault testing in pre-energization. During energization it has you verify correct operate and restraint quantities to the differential protection. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.2.A.33, 7.2.A.34, 7.2.B.7.

question: A new feeder lineup is being commissioned. Under ECS Section 9, the thermographic survey should be done at:
choices: Any load, since delta-T is independent of current
Normal circuit loading, with no minimum
No load, to get a clean baseline
Maximum possible load, at least 40% of nominal
explanation: ECS asks for maximum possible loading but no less than 40% of nominal, referring to NFPA 70B. ATS Section 9 says normal circuit loading. MTS says maximum possible loading with no stated floor. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 9.3.3; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 9; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Section 9.
reference: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 9.3.3; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 9; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Section 9

question: At turnover under ECS-2024 Section 10, what happens to the commissioning organization's locks and tags?
choices: They stay on until the first maintenance outage
Removed and replaced by operator locks and tags
They are transferred to the owner without change
They are removed only after the warranty expires
explanation: Turnover is formal and documented. The operator is told about outstanding deficiencies and abnormal conditions, gets the documentation, and the commissioning locks and tags are replaced by the operator's where needed. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 10.

question: During energization of a new automatic transfer switch, ECS 8.3 has you do a load transfer test. What is checked besides the fact that the load moves?
choices: That the generator's PI is above 2.0
That the transfer time meets the project requirements
That the switch passes a 10-minute insulation-resistance test
That the normal source fails within 1 cycle
explanation: ECS asks you to transfer the actual connected load and monitor the transfer time against the specified project requirements. With several transfer switches or other protective devices, coordination tests verify the sequencing too. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 8.3.B.10 and B.11.

question: A PDU is fed from a UPS. The UPS has an input breaker, a battery breaker, a static-bypass input, and a maintenance bypass. A tech opens and locks only the UPS input breaker and calls the PDU dead. What did he miss?
choices: The battery and bypass paths are also sources
Nothing, since the UPS input is the only utility connection
Only the battery breaker; the bypass paths are interlocked
Only the downstream PDU main; the UPS is upstream
explanation: Establishing an electrically safe work condition starts with finding every possible source from current drawings, then opening a disconnect for each. A UPS has several: the inverter on battery, the static bypass, and the maintenance bypass. Source: NFPA 70E-2024 120.6(1) and 120.6(2).

question: What makes breaker-failure relaying (50BF) different from remote backup protection?
choices: It replaces the primary relay on the feeder
It only operates when the dc battery has failed
It closes the failed breaker again after a short time delay
It catches a stuck breaker locally, not remotely
explanation: IEEE 242 calls breaker-failure relaying local breaker backup. Remote backup relies on relays at other terminals and is slower and less selective. When testing 50BF, ATS 7.9.1 covers current-supervision pickup, time delays, and the initiate inputs and trip outputs. Source: IEEE 242-2001, 14.5.7; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1.

question: Before connecting a test set to an in-service relay, in what order does Werstiuk recommend isolating and restoring circuits?
choices: Isolate ac first, then trip; on restore, put trip back first
Trip circuit out first; on restore, ac back first, then trip
Leave the trip circuit in so you can see a real breaker operation
Isolate only the ac circuits; the trip circuit doesn't matter
explanation: Disabling the trip path first keeps a nuisance trip from happening as ac circuits are disturbed. On restore, ac goes back first so you can confirm no trip signals are present before the trip and close circuits are put back. Source: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, 1.
reference: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, 1

question: A tech wants to time a relay by putting the test set's timer input across the relay's trip contact while the trip circuit is still connected. Werstiuk's warning is that:
choices: The timer will read the ac ripple and give false times
A low-impedance timer input can trip the breaker
The relay will lock out its own targets
The dc will damage the relay's output contact
explanation: Some test-set sensing inputs act almost like a jumper. Across a live trip contact they can energize the trip coil. Isolate the trip circuit or use a connection that can't complete it. Source: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, Figure 18-4.
reference: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, Figure 18-4

question: In a short-circuit study, which calculated current is used to check the interrupting duty of low-voltage breakers and fuses?
choices: The 30-cycle time-delayed current
The interrupting-network current used for MV breakers
The steady-state load-flow current
The first-cycle (half-cycle) current
explanation: IEEE 399 explains that the first-cycle network gives the momentary (close-and-latch) duty for MV and HV gear, while for LV gear that same result is the duty the device must interrupt. The interrupting-network results are used for MV and HV breakers. Source: IEEE 399-1997, 7.4.1 and Table 7-2 notes.

question: Time-delayed short-circuit currents (beyond 6 cycles, up to 30) are used to check time-overcurrent relay sensitivity. How does IEEE 399 model motors for that case?
choices: Motor contributions are left out
Motors are modeled with subtransient reactance
Motor contribution is doubled for safety
Only induction motors above 50 hp are included
explanation: By then motor contributions have decayed, so they are left out, and generators use transient or higher reactance. These currents also carry no dc offset. Source: IEEE 399-1997, 7.4.1.

question: A plant changes relay settings on its main breakers but changes no equipment. Under MTS Appendix C, which study is not marked for update?
choices: The coordination study
The incident-energy analysis
The short-circuit study
The one-line diagram
explanation: A change in protective devices or settings marks the one-line, coordination, incident energy, and load flow. Fault current doesn't change when only settings change, so the short-circuit study isn't marked. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: A plant adds several large motors to an existing bus. Under MTS Appendix C (change in impedance, configuration, or loading), which updates are marked?
choices: All five studies
Only coordination and load flow, nothing else at all
One-line, short-circuit, and incident energy
Incident energy only
explanation: That row marks the one-line, short-circuit, and incident-energy columns. Motor additions are one of the note 1 examples because motors contribute fault current. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C and note 1.
reference: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C and note 1

question: MTS Appendix B base interval for full electrical testing of a liquid-filled transformer is 24 months. The unit is in poor condition and serves a high-reliability load. The adjusted interval is:
choices: 6 months
12 months
24 months
60 months
explanation: The Appendix B matrix factor for high reliability and poor condition is 0.25. 24 x 0.25 = 6 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: A medium-voltage breaker has a 36-month base interval for full electrical testing. It is in good condition on a low-reliability-requirement circuit. Using MTS Appendix B, the interval becomes:
choices: 18 months
36 months
54 months
90 months
explanation: Low reliability with good condition has a factor of 2.5. 36 x 2.5 = 90 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: A microprocessor relay has a 36-month base interval for electrical testing. It is in average condition and protects a high-reliability process. Using MTS Appendix B, test it every:
choices: 9 months
18 months
36 months
72 months
explanation: High reliability with average condition has a factor of 0.50. 36 x 0.5 = 18 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: On industrial machinery, the protective bonding circuit is checked with an impedance instrument. What is the NFPA 79 maximum?
choices: 1 ohm
0.1 ohm, allowing for the test lead impedance
25 ohms
0.5 megohm
explanation: With the impedance-meter method, the effective ground-fault current path must measure 0.1 ohm or less once the test circuit's own impedance is taken out. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.2(1).

question: Using the NFPA 79 10 A method on a 14 AWG protective conductor, what is the largest voltage drop allowed?
explanation: The alternative continuity method drives at least 10 A at 50 or 60 Hz from a SELV source and measures the drop. Table 18.2 sets the limit by wire size, and for 14 AWG it is 1.9 V. Thinner wire is allowed more. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.2(2) and Table 18.2.

question: When NFPA 79 insulation resistance testing applies, what test voltage and minimum value are used?
choices: 500 V dc, at least 1 megohm between power conductors and the protective bonding circuit
1000 V dc, at least 100 megohms
250 V dc, at least 0.5 megohm
2500 V dc, at least 25 megohms
explanation: Apply 500 V dc between the power circuit conductors and the ground-fault path. The reading must be at least 1 megohm. Sections of a large machine may be tested one at a time. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.3.

question: An NFPA 79 voltage test is applied to a machine's primary circuits. Which setup matches the standard?
choices: Apply 2121 V ac for 1 minute
Apply 1000 V dc instantly for 10 minutes
Raise gradually to 1500 V ac, or its 2121 V dc peak equivalent, and hold at least 1 s, from a supply of at least 500 VA
Apply 500 V ac for 1 s from any source
explanation: Bring the voltage up from zero to 1500 V ac, or the 2121 V dc equivalent, from the primary conductors to the ground-fault path, and hold at least one second without breakdown. 1500 × √2 ≈ 2121, which is why those numbers pair. Disconnect parts that can't take the voltage. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.4.

question: A machine's wiring was modified in the field. Which NFPA 79 verification is always required, and what about the rest?
choices: All five tests are mandatory on every machine every time
Only the voltage test is required
Ground-fault path continuity is always verified and documented; the other tests are done where they apply, and changed parts are retested
Nothing, if the machine was listed
explanation: The ground-fault return path is always proved continuous and written up. Insulation, voltage, residual-voltage and function tests happen when judged necessary. After a change, the affected portion is re-verified. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.1 and 18.7.

question: A stationary fuel cell room has combustible gas detection. Under NFPA 853, at what levels does it alarm and shut off the fuel?
choices: Alarm at 25% of the LFL; shut off fuel at 60% of the LFL
Alarm at 10% LFL; shut off at 25% LFL
Alarm at 50% LFL; shut off at 100% LFL
Alarm only; no fuel shutoff
explanation: The detector alarms at a quarter of the lowest lower flammable limit for the gas and closes the fuel supply at 60%. Put the detectors where leaks are likely for the fuel used. Source: NFPA 853-2025, 8.1.5.4 to 8.1.5.7.

question: At a generating plant, two outdoor oil-filled transformers sit near each other. Under NFPA 850, how is the separation decided?
choices: No separation is ever needed outdoors
Only by the transformer maker's catalog
By NFPA 70B maintenance intervals
By the documented fire protection design basis, with fire barriers, distance or another approved method (Table 6.1.4.3)
explanation: Outdoor oil-insulated transformers are kept apart from each other and from buildings by fire barriers, distance or another approved method. The analysis is recorded in the fire protection design basis document, and the table gives the 2-hour firewall or spacing options. Source: NFPA 850-2026, 6.1.4.1 to 6.1.4.3 and Table 6.1.4.3.

question: A project is still in design, and the owner asks when the commissioning plan should be written and who should write it. What does ANSI/NETA ECS require?
choices: The installing contractor writes the plan after energization, and it is never updated
The plan is written only during occupancy, after punch-list work is complete
The commissioning authority should write the plan while the project is still in design, then the team should keep it current through construction, acceptance, and occupancy
The authority having jurisdiction must author the plan during factory testing
explanation: ECS has the commissioning authority write the plan while the project is still in design, and has the team keep that plan current through construction, acceptance, and occupancy. Waiting until after energization is too late for the plan to guide the work. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, 6.4.

question: Two versions of the commissioning plan are in circulation: last month's draft on a technician's laptop and a later revision on the project site. The crew is about to start functional tests from the laptop copy. What should you require?
choices: Stop and have everyone work from the most up-to-date version of the commissioning plan
Either copy is fine if the equipment list looks similar
Field crews should prefer the oldest plan because it was issued in design
Functional tests do not have to follow the commissioning plan
explanation: ECS requires parties involved in executing the commissioning plan to work from the most up-to-date version. A stale draft can omit later tests, sequence changes, or owner revisions. Resolve the version issue before the tests proceed. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, 6.4.

question: You are reviewing a commissioning plan and need to confirm that it describes the work around energization. Which set of activities does ECS say the plan should generally describe?
choices: Only post-energization monitoring; pre-energization work is outside the plan
Only factory tests; field energization is not part of commissioning
Only occupancy-phase training, with no description of energization work
The work that will be done before, during, and after energization
explanation: ECS lists the contents of the commissioning plan, including a general description of the work before, during, and after energization. A plan that skips those activities is incomplete for a senior technician who has to develop or review it. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, 6.4.

question: An owner document lists project goals, how the facility will be used, measurable performance criteria, and success measures. A second document records the concepts, calculations, product selections, and code decisions used to meet that first document. How should you tell them apart?
choices: The first is the Basis of Design and the second is the Owner's Project Requirements
The first is the Owner's Project Requirements. The second is the Basis of Design, which is the record of how the design meets those requirements and the applicable rules
Both documents are commissioning plans, and the names can be used interchangeably
The first is a factory test procedure and the second is an as-built drawing list
explanation: ECS, following the ASHRAE Guideline 0 usage it cites, treats the Owner's Project Requirements as the written statement of functional needs and how the project will be used and operated, including what the owner wants the project to achieve, how success will be measured, cost limits, and supporting information. The Basis of Design is the record of the concepts, calculations, product choices, and code decisions used to satisfy those needs and the applicable rules. A senior technician reviewing scope has to know which document is which. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, 6.2 and 6.3.

question: Component tests on a new lineup have all passed, and the crew wants to call the job complete without system function tests because every relay and breaker was already tested on the bench. What is the right call?
choices: Bench tests of each device are a complete substitute for system function tests
Require system function tests. They are how you show that sensing, processing, and action devices work together correctly, and ATS says to perform them following ECS
System function tests are only used in maintenance, not at acceptance
System function tests can be skipped when insulation resistance is acceptable
explanation: ATS describes system function tests as the way to show that sensing, processing, and action devices work together correctly, and it points those tests at ECS. Passing isolated component tests does not prove that the devices work together as a system. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, Section 8; ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, Section 6.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, Section 8; ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, Section 6

question: Factory and field acceptance reports on a new substation still list open deficiencies. A superintendent wants to energize anyway and finish the paperwork later. What should you do?
choices: Energize now; deficiencies can always be closed after the system is live
Only factory reports matter; field deficiencies can be ignored
Energization is allowed as long as a commissioning plan exists, even if it was never followed
Do not energize until factory and field acceptance records, including open deficiencies, have been reviewed and the equipment is in acceptable condition and is ready for first energization
explanation: ECS includes a review of factory and field acceptance records, including open deficiencies, so you can confirm the equipment is in acceptable condition and is ready for first energization and for final acceptance. Open deficiencies that affect suitability are not a paperwork exercise to be finished after the equipment is already live. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, Section 6.

question: A Category IV transformer will be applied on a feeder that recloses. The short-circuit study is being used to judge through-fault duty. Which duration check belongs in that review?
choices: Confirm that the total time of repeated through-faults from reclosing stays within the two-second single-event limit that applies to Category II through IV units unless the user specified another duration
Ignore reclosing; only the first fault counts for Category IV
Allow up to 30 seconds of accumulated fault time on any Category IV unit
Category IV has no short-circuit duration limit in C57.12.00
explanation: IEEE C57.12.00 limits the defined short-circuit duration for Category II, III, and IV units to two seconds unless the user specifies otherwise, and it requires transformers on reclosing circuits to ride through repeated faults so long as the total time stays within that single-event maximum. Applying a study on a reclosing feeder means checking that accumulated duty, not only the first shot. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 7.1.3.1.

question: After a feeder fault, the event record shows the downstream device should have cleared first, but the upstream main opened instead. Drawings, the coordination study, and the as-left settings have not been compared. What should you do first?
choices: Raise the main pickup immediately so it cannot trip again
Replace the downstream breaker without looking at the study or the event record
Review the documentation, the coordination study, and the as-left settings, and analyze the event record before you recommend a corrective action or change a setting
Ignore the event record; documentation review is only a design-phase task
explanation: Senior-level troubleshooting starts with documentation and event information, then a cause, then a recommended correction. Changing a setting or swapping a device before the study and the as-left settings are compared to the event can make coordination worse. ECS and the Level IV systems outline both expect that review-and-recommend sequence. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, Section 6; IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 15.

question: Temporary meters on a 480 V bus show flat-topped voltage and elevated current in a capacitor bank next to a large rectifier, while transformers on the same bus are running hotter than the kVA load would suggest. What is the most useful first recommendation?
choices: Add more capacitors immediately to correct power factor; heating will then stop
Ignore the rectifier; capacitor heating is almost always a loose bolt only
Treat this as a harmonic problem from the nonlinear load, keep the monitoring in place long enough to characterize it, and recommend a study or mitigation before adding more capacitors
Remove all metering; a single snapshot is enough to close a power-quality complaint
explanation: Level IV systems work includes power-quality monitoring and recognizing anomalies. Nonlinear loads inject harmonic current. Capacitors have falling impedance with frequency and can absorb a large share of that current and overheat, and transformers see extra heating as well. Adding capacitors without characterizing the harmonic environment can make the condition worse. Temporary monitoring should be used to support the recommendation. Source: IEEE 519-2022; IEEE 141-1993, Chapter 8.

question: You are reviewing a coordination plot before a main-breaker test. The study shows the feeder's curve clearing below the main, with a coordinating interval between them. The field setting sheet on the main is faster than the study. What do you do?
choices: Install the faster field setting; a shorter time is always safer
Ignore the study because field technicians do not apply study data
Raise both pickups until the two curves overlap completely
Hold the test and get the setting reconciled with the coordination study before you energize or apply the field setting
explanation: Level IV theory includes reading coordination curves and applying data from short-circuit and coordination studies. If the field setting does not match the study, the coordination you think you have is not the coordination that will be in service. Resolve the mismatch with the engineer or the study author before the equipment goes on the line. Source: IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 15; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.4 and 8.4.2.H.6.

question: A plant adds a large transformer and several motors but no one updates the short-circuit study. You are asked to accept a new breaker using the old interrupting-duty numbers. What is the right call?
choices: Do not accept the old numbers. A change in system impedance, configuration, or loading is a reason to update the short-circuit study before you apply those values
The old study is fine for five more years regardless of changes
Only the coordination study needs an update; short-circuit duty never changes when motors are added
You can scale the old duties by nameplate kVA and skip a new study
explanation: MTS Appendix C lists the conditions that call for updating power-system studies, including a change in impedance, configuration, or loading. Added transformers and motors change available fault current and motor contribution. Interrupting ratings taken from a study that no longer represents the system are not a basis for acceptance. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, Appendix C; IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.6 and 8.4.2.H.9.
reference: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, Appendix C; IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.6 and 8.4.2.H.9

question: A coordination study is being applied to set a low-voltage breaker that must also meet its interrupting rating. Which calculated current from the short-circuit study is used to check that interrupting duty?
choices: Only the 30-cycle current, because low-voltage breakers are slow
The transformer inrush current from the last energization
The first-cycle (momentary) or interrupting-duty current the study produces for that bus, including motor contribution as the study specifies
The arcing current from an incident-energy study, in place of bolted-fault current
explanation: Short-circuit studies produce different current values for different purposes. Interrupting duty for low-voltage breakers and fuses is checked with the appropriate first-cycle or interrupting current from the study, including motor contribution where the study applies it. Time-delayed currents are used for other checks, such as overcurrent-relay sensitivity, not as a substitute for interrupting duty. Source: IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 2; IEEE 399-1997, Chapter 6; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.5 and 8.4.2.H.6.
reference: IEEE 242-2001, Chapter 2; IEEE 399-1997, Chapter 6; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.5 and 8.4.2.H.6

question: A plant wants to parallel a standard delta-wye transformer with a standard delta-delta transformer of the same voltage. What angular relationship should you expect, and can they be paralleled?
choices: A standard delta-wye (or wye-delta) unit has the high side 30 degrees ahead of the low side, while a standard delta-delta or wye-wye unit has a 0 degree shift. A delta-wye transformer cannot be paralleled with a delta-delta or wye-wye transformer
All standard three-phase transformers have a 0 degree shift, so any two of the same voltage may be paralleled
Standard delta-wye and delta-delta units both shift 30 degrees and may be paralleled without a phasing check
A standard wye-wye unit cannot be paralleled with a standard delta-delta unit because of a 30 degree shift
explanation: On standard delta-wye and wye-delta transformers the high-voltage phases lead the low-voltage phases by 30 degrees. On standard delta-delta and wye-wye transformers that lead is 0 degrees. Therefore a standard delta-wye can be paralleled with a standard wye-delta (aside from the lack of a grounded neutral on a delta secondary), and a wye-wye can be paralleled with a delta-delta. A delta-wye cannot be paralleled with a delta-delta or a wye-wye. Older nonstandard banks can have other shifts, including 150 degrees. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on standard three-phase transformers.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on standard three-phase transformers

question: A replacement transformer is energized and ready to be tied. A phase-sequence (rotation) meter on each bus shows ABC. The crew wants to close the tie on that basis. What does Lautenschlager require before the buses are paralleled?
choices: Matching rotation readings are sufficient, and a voltmeter check across the open tie is unnecessary
An oscilloscope or phase-angle meter is mandatory; a voltmeter cannot verify phasing
If both buses are labeled A-B-C, the nameplates alone are enough to close the tie

A rotation meter is not enough to prove the buses are in phase. Confirm that the voltage between each pair of corresponding phases is zero, or nearly zero, using a voltmeter or phasing sticks rated for the system
explanation: Phasing is proven by measuring voltage across each pair of like-named phases on the two buses and getting a reading of zero, or essentially zero. A rotation or sequence meter cannot make that call, and you do not need one for the check; that instrument is for confirming motor direction after a reconnection. Lead versus lag can be seen on a phase-angle meter or a scope, but those tools are optional. A voltmeter or phasing sticks rated for the voltage is all that is required. Do not trust phase letters alone; they often do not line up from one system to the next. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on what phasing is.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on what phasing is

question: With both secondaries at the same phase-to-phase voltage, you measure phase-to-ground voltage between each pair of correspondingly named phases across an open tie. About what displacement does Lautenschlager's Table 1 assign to that reading?
choices: Phase-to-ground voltage between correspondingly named phases means the buses are in phase
About 60 degrees. Zero volts means in phase, phase-to-phase voltage means about 120 degrees, and twice phase-to-ground voltage means 180 degrees
Phase-to-ground voltage means 180 degrees of displacement
Phase-to-ground voltage cannot be related to a displacement angle; only a phase-angle meter can be used
explanation: Lautenschlager's Table 1 converts a voltage taken between like-named phases — assuming the two buses have the same line-to-line voltage — into an angle. A near-zero reading means the buses are in step. About half of line-to-ground voltage points to 30 degrees; a line-to-ground reading to 60 degrees; about 1.4 times line-to-ground to 90 degrees; a line-to-line reading to 120 degrees; about 1.9 times line-to-ground to 150 degrees; and twice line-to-ground to 180 degrees. Scattered, inconsistent readings usually mean at least one side is ungrounded. Those voltages will not tell you which side leads. Load can nudge the field numbers a little off the table. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1

question: Two transformers will be paralleled on a common secondary bus. Before you even start the phasing measurements, which two nameplate checks does Lautenschlager say to make, and why?
choices: Only the kVA ratings need to match; tap position and percent impedance do not affect load sharing

Confirm they are on the same voltage tap, and that each transformer's percent impedance is between 92.5% and 107.5% of the other. The unit with the higher secondary voltage or the lower percent impedance will take more of the load once the buses are tied
The transformer with the higher percent impedance will always take more load, so mismatch is desirable
Tap position may differ freely as long as the percent impedances are identical
explanation: Do the nameplate checks before any phasing shots. Both units should be on matching taps; a unit left on a higher tap will pick up extra load once the tie is closed. Percent impedance should also stay inside 92.5% to 107.5% of the companion unit. The stiffer transformer — the one with the smaller percent impedance — holds up better under load and therefore takes a larger share after the buses are joined. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on steps before attempting to perform phasing.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on steps before attempting to perform phasing

question: Across an open tie you measure phase-to-phase voltage between every pair of correspondingly named phases. Both systems have the same rotation. What is the displacement, and how is it corrected?
choices: The buses are 180 degrees apart, and the only fix is to reverse the polarity of all three secondary windings
The buses are in phase; the phase-to-phase reading is expected when rotation matches
Swap only two leads on a delta-wye secondary; a full A-B-C rotation is never used for a 120 degree case
The buses are 120 degrees apart. Move the leads on one system so that what was A becomes B, B becomes C, and C becomes A. If they are still 120 degrees out, repeat that rotation once more
explanation: Situation 2 is a 120 degree displacement with the same rotation, shown by a phase-to-phase voltage between each pair of correspondingly named phases. It is typically a transformer or tie-switch lead sequence error. Correct it by rotating the leads on one side — at the bank primary or secondary, or at the switch — so A is moved to the old B position, B to C, and C to A. If the buses are still 120 degrees apart, do that rotation one more time. A phase-angle meter would show which way to shift, but it is not required. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 2.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 2

question: Two buses served through wye-delta transformers show phase-to-phase voltage on two correspondingly named pairs and zero volts on the third pair. What does that pattern indicate, and what is the correction?
choices: The two systems have opposing rotation, typically from two leads reversed on a wye-delta transformer. Exchange the primary or secondary (or switch) leads on the two phases that showed the phase-to-phase voltage
The systems are in phase on all three and may be paralleled immediately
This is the signature of a 30 degree connection mismatch that cannot be corrected by swapping leads
Exchange the two leads on the phase that read zero volts, and leave the other two alone
explanation: Situation 3 is phase-to-phase voltage (120 degrees) between two correspondingly named buses and zero volts on the third. That pattern means the systems have opposing rotation, and it occurs with wye-delta transformers when two leads are reversed. The correction is to swap the bank primary leads, or the bank secondary leads, or the switch leads, on the two phases that showed the phase-to-phase voltage. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 3.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 3

question: On a double-ended 480 V substation, you measure phase-to-ground voltage (60 degrees) between all three correspondingly named buses of the two secondaries. The transformers face each other and are not a mirror-image pair. What typical connection error does Lautenschlager describe, and how is it corrected?
choices: The buses are in phase; a 60 degree reading on all three is the expected result for two identical delta-wye units
Reverse the polarity of one secondary wye only; the primaries should be left as found

One transformer is incorrectly phased relative to the other, often because a standard unit replaced a mirror-image unit. Exchange two primary leads and the same two secondary leads. Exchanging only the primary leaves the secondaries wrong
This pattern cannot be corrected in the field; both transformers must be replaced
explanation: Situation 5 is a phase-to-ground (60 degree) reading between each of the three buses, seen on the 480 V side of a double-ended substation when one of two delta-wye transformers is incorrectly connected. If the two units are the same design, not a mirror pair, and face each other, the second unit may have primary A on H3 and C on H1, and secondary a on X3 and c on X1. The correction is to exchange two primary leads and the same two secondary leads. It does not matter which pair is exchanged, except that if H1 and H2 are swapped, X1 and X2 must be swapped as well. Exchanging the 480 V leads is often the hard part. This commonly happens when a standard transformer replaces a nonstandard unit that was built as a mirror pair (H1 with H3, and X1 with X3, reversed). Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 5.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 5

question: Readings across an open tie are consistently about 0.5, 1.4, or 1.9 times line-to-ground voltage, corresponding to 30, 90, or 150 degrees. What does that tell you about paralleling, and what transfer option remains if all three readings are the same and the rotations match?
choices: A 30 degree difference is close enough to parallel if the percent impedances match
Any 30, 90, or 150 degree pattern can be corrected by rolling the leads once, after which the buses may be paralleled

The two systems have different phase relationships (typically delta-wye or wye-delta on one side and delta-delta or wye-wye on the other) and cannot be paralleled. If all three readings are the same and the rotations match, motor loads may still be transferred by dropping one source and picking the loads up on the other
If rotations match, the buses may be paralleled regardless of those displacement voltages
explanation: Situation 7 is the 30-, 90-, or 150-degree case, which typically means one side is a wye-delta or delta-wye bank and the other is delta-delta or wye-wye. Those sources must not be tied together. When every pair shows the same one of those three angles, rotation matches, so motors can be moved by opening one source and then closing the other. That is a break-before-make transfer, not a parallel. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 7.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 7

question: Voltages measured between correspondingly named phases of two buses are inconsistent, and one or both systems appear ungrounded. After you confirm that, how does Lautenschlager say to finish the phasing check, and what voltage hazard appears if the wrong phases are tied when only one system is grounded?
choices: Land a fused jumper, rated only for charging current, on the like-named phase of each ungrounded bus and take the three shots again; the jumpered pair should already read zero. When only one side already has a ground, a wrong-phase jumper can drive the remaining ungrounded phases to 2.0 times, and 2.75 times, their usual line-to-ground voltage
Inconsistent voltages mean the buses are in phase and may be paralleled without temporary grounds
An ungrounded bus cannot be phased at all and must be left isolated
Tying the wrong phases of a grounded and an ungrounded system only produces a 30 degree error, with no overvoltage
explanation: Scattered readings usually mean one bus, or both, has no ground reference. Confirm that by looking at each bus's line-to-ground voltages; capacitance unbalance on an ungrounded bus can push those readings above twice line-to-line voltage. When both sides are ungrounded, land a fused jumper — rated only for charging current — on the same phase of each bus, then take the three shots. If the buses may be tied, the three readings should be essentially zero, and the pair you jumpered is already at zero. Pull the jumpers before closing the tie. When only one side is grounded, you can still phase by joining one like-named phase and reading the other two, but a wrong-phase jumper can drive the remaining ungrounded phases to 2.0 times, and 2.75 times, their usual line-to-ground voltage. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 8.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Situation 8

question: Before closing a tie between two 480Y/277 V buses, you read 392 V from A on one bus to A on the other, and the same on B and C. What is the angle between the systems, and what can you tell about lead or lag?
choices: About 90 degrees (a bit over 1.4 x the 277 V line-to-ground value). Lead or lag cannot be told from voltage readings alone
About 30 degrees, and bus 1 leads
About 120 degrees, which is a simple lead rotation
About 90 degrees, and bus 2 lags, because the reading is below 480 V
explanation: Across like phases, the voltage is 2 x VLG x sin(angle / 2). 392 / 277 is about 1.41, and 2 x sin 45 degrees is 1.414, so the angle is about 90 degrees. Lautenschlager's Table 1 puts 90 degrees at a bit over 1.4 x VLG and notes that leading and lagging cannot be found from voltage measurements. A phase-angle meter or scope can show it. Do not parallel. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4

question: Using phasing sticks on a 12.47Y/7.2 kV tie, you read about 12.47 kV between like phases on all three pairs, and both systems show the same rotation. What does that mean, and what is the fix?
choices: The systems are 180 degrees apart; swap any two leads
The systems are in phase, because the reading equals the nominal voltage
The systems have opposite rotation; swap two leads on one side
The systems are 120 degrees apart with the same rotation. Roll the three leads on one side one position (A to the B position, and so on) and phase again; repeat once more if still 120 degrees
explanation: A reading equal to phase-to-phase voltage between like phases is the 120 degree row of Lautenschlager's Table 1 (2 x 7.2 x sin 60 degrees is about 12.47 kV). With the same rotation on all three pairs, this is Situation 2: shift the leads on one system one position and phase again. Opposite rotation shows a different pattern, with two pairs at phase-to-phase and one pair at zero. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1 and Situation 2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1 and Situation 2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4

question: On a 4160Y/2400 V system you are told the two sources may be 60 degrees apart. What reading between like phases should you expect if that is true?
choices: About 4160 V, equal to phase-to-phase voltage
About 2400 V, equal to the phase-to-ground voltage
About 1200 V, half of phase-to-ground
About 4800 V, twice phase-to-ground
explanation: 2 x VLG x sin(60 / 2) = 2 x 2400 x 0.5 = 2400 V. Lautenschlager's Table 1 lists phase-to-ground voltage for a 60 degree displacement, phase-to-phase for 120 degrees, and twice phase-to-ground for 180 degrees. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, Table 1; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4

question: Two transformers on the same tap will be paralleled. One is 5.75% Z. Using the Lautenschlager pre-phasing check, which impedance range is acceptable for the other unit, and is 6.25% inside it?
choices: About 5.25% to 6.25%, so 6.25% is acceptable
About 5.32% to 6.18%, so 6.25% is outside the window
About 5.00% to 6.50%, so 6.25% is acceptable
Any impedance is fine if the taps match
explanation: Lautenschlager asks that one transformer's %Z be within 92.5% to 107.5% of the other's. 0.925 x 5.75 = 5.32% and 1.075 x 5.75 = 6.18%. A 6.25% unit is about 108.7% of 5.75, just outside. The lower-%Z unit holds up its voltage better under load and takes more of the load. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on checks before phasing; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on checks before phasing; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4

question: Two 1000 kVA transformers on the same tap, 5.0% Z and 6.0% Z, are paralleled to carry 1800 kVA. Treating the impedances as current dividers on the same base, about how is the load split?
choices: 900 kVA each, because the ratings match
About 818 kVA on the 5.0% unit and 982 kVA on the 6.0% unit
About 1500 kVA on the 5.0% unit and 300 kVA on the 6.0% unit
About 982 kVA on the 5.0% unit and 818 kVA on the 6.0% unit
explanation: Parallel paths share current in inverse proportion to their impedance. The 5.0% unit carries 1800 x 6.0 / (5.0 + 6.0), about 982 kVA, and the 6.0% unit carries 1800 x 5.0 / 11, about 818 kVA. That fits Lautenschlager's point that the lower-%Z transformer carries more of the load. Here the 5% unit is about 98% loaded while the other is about 82%. Source: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on checks before phasing; Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 2.6 and 2.10; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4.
reference: Lautenschlager, A Guide to Paralleling Electrical Systems, NETA World, Fall 2008, section on checks before phasing; Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 2.6 and 2.10; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.A.4
